title: Arithmetic: hours watched
name: Hours Watched
prompt: Reports at Driftlight show viewing time in hours. Create Hours Watched: the minutes watched in each session, in hours.
hints: Field names go in square brackets: [Minutes Watched].
There are 60 minutes in an hour, so divide.
debrief: This is a row-level calculation: Tableau computes it for every session, then aggregates it in the view like any other measure (SUM(Hours Watched)). Because it returns a number, Tableau puts it under Measures in the Data pane.

title: Arithmetic: price with tax
name: Price with Tax
prompt: Finance wants each subscriber's monthly price including 20% sales tax, rounded to cents (2 decimal places).
hints: Adding 20% is the same as multiplying by 1.2.
ROUND(number, decimals) rounds to a number of decimal places.
debrief: ROUND's second argument is the number of decimal places; leave it out to round to a whole number. Rounding inside the calculation changes the stored values; a number format only changes how they are shown.

title: Nulls: count missing minutes as zero
name: Minutes (0 if missing)
prompt: A few sessions have no Minutes Watched recorded (the field is null). Create a field that gives the minutes watched, or 0 where they are missing.
hints: Arithmetic with a null gives null, so [Minutes Watched] + 0 is still null.
ZN(expression) returns the value, or zero when it is null. IFNULL(expr1, expr2) works too.
debrief: ZN is a special case of IFNULL with 0 as the replacement. Use it when a missing value really means zero; when it means unknown, leaving the null keeps averages honest, because AVG ignores nulls but counts zeros.

title: Logic: session length bands
name: Session Length
prompt: Label each session "Short" (under 30 minutes), "Medium" (30 to under 90) or "Long" (90 or more). Sessions without minutes recorded should be "Unknown".
expected: IF ISNULL([Minutes Watched]) THEN "Unknown" ELSEIF [Minutes Watched] < 30 THEN "Short" ELSEIF [Minutes Watched] < 90 THEN "Medium" ELSE "Long" END
accepted: IF ISNULL([Minutes Watched]) THEN 'Unknown' ELSEIF [Minutes Watched] >= 90 THEN 'Long' ELSEIF [Minutes Watched] >= 30 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Short' END
IFNULL(IF [Minutes Watched] < 30 THEN 'Short' ELSEIF [Minutes Watched] < 90 THEN 'Medium' ELSEIF [Minutes Watched] >= 90 THEN 'Long' END, 'Unknown')
wrong: IF [Minutes Watched] < 30 THEN 'Short' ELSEIF [Minutes Watched] < 90 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Long' END
IF ISNULL([Minutes Watched]) THEN 'Unknown' ELSEIF [Minutes Watched] <= 30 THEN 'Short' ELSEIF [Minutes Watched] < 90 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Long' END
hints: The form is IF test THEN value ELSEIF test THEN value ELSE value END.
Test for the missing minutes first with ISNULL([Minutes Watched]): a comparison with a null is null, and IF sends a null test to ELSE.
debrief: The tests run top to bottom and the first true one wins, so each ELSEIF only sees what the earlier tests let through. An IF whose test is null takes the ELSE branch, which is why the null check comes first. The result is a string, so the new field is a dimension you can put on Rows or Color.

title: Logic: ad tier with IIF
name: Ad Tier
prompt: Label each subscriber "With ads" when their plan is ad supported and "Ad-free" otherwise. Use IIF.
accepted: IF [Ad Supported] THEN 'With ads' ELSE 'Ad-free' END
hints: IIF(test, then, else): the test can be a Boolean field on its own.
Ad Supported is already TRUE or FALSE, so you don't need = TRUE.
debrief: IIF is a compact IF with one test. It also takes an optional fourth argument for when the test is null; without it, a null test gives Null.

title: String: city and country
name: Location
prompt: Create a label like "Seattle, United States": the subscriber's city, a comma and a space, then the country.
hints: The + operator joins strings.
Put the separator in quotes: ", " (a comma and a space).
debrief: + adds numbers and joins strings, but it can't mix them: to join a number to text, convert it with STR() first.

title: String: the number in an ID
name: Subscriber Number
prompt: Subscriber IDs look like SUB-00002. Create Subscriber Number: the digits after the dash, kept as text ("00002").
hints: MID(string, start) returns everything from position start, and the first character is position 1.
S-U-B-dash is four characters, so the digits start at position 5. RIGHT or SPLIT work too.
debrief: String positions in Tableau start at 1. SPLIT(string, delimiter, token) is handy for IDs and codes: a negative token counts from the right.

title: String: titles that start with “The”
name: Starts with The
prompt: Flag the titles whose name starts with the word "The" followed by a space (TRUE or FALSE).
hints: STARTSWITH(string, substring) returns TRUE or FALSE.
Include the space, so a title such as "Theory of Tides" wouldn't count.
debrief: A calculation that returns TRUE or FALSE is a Boolean dimension: drop it on Color or Filters to split the titles in two.

title: Date: hour of the day
name: Start Hour
prompt: The product team wants to see when people watch. Create Start Hour: the hour (0 to 23) each session started, as a number.
hints: DATEPART(date_part, date) returns a part of a date as a whole number.
The date part is written as text: 'hour'.
debrief: DATEPART returns a number, DATENAME the same part as text, and DATETRUNC a date cut back to the start of the part. A number calc lands under Measures; to use Start Hour as a header, convert it to a dimension or make it discrete.

title: Date: the month a subscriber joined
name: Signup Month
prompt: Create Signup Month: the signup date cut back to the first day of its month (2024-10-17 becomes 2024-10-01), still a date.
hints: You want a date back, not a month number.
DATETRUNC(date_part, date) cuts a date back to the start of the part.
debrief: DATETRUNC gives a date value, like a continuous date pill set to Month, while DATEPART('month', …) gives 1 to 12, like a discrete MONTH part that mixes every year's March together.

title: Date: days until cancellation
name: Days to Cancel
prompt: For subscribers who cancelled, create Days to Cancel: the number of days from Signup Date to Cancel Date. Subscribers who never cancelled have no Cancel Date, so their value stays null.
hints: DATEDIFF(date_part, start date, end date).
Put the earlier date first, or the result is negative.
debrief: DATEDIFF counts how many date parts lie between two dates, from the first argument to the second. A null date makes the result null, so the subscribers who never cancelled drop out of averages instead of counting as zero.

title: Date: months since signup
name: Months Subscribed
prompt: Create Months Subscribed: how many months lie between each subscriber's Signup Date and today. In this playground TODAY() is fixed at January 1, 2026, so the answers never change.
hints: TODAY() takes no argument and returns today's date.
Use DATEDIFF with 'month', the earlier date first.
debrief: TODAY() makes a calculation move with the calendar: in Tableau the same workbook gives a new answer tomorrow. That's what you want for "days since" fields, and why exercises here pin it.

title: Date: weekend sessions
name: Weekend
prompt: Flag the sessions that started on a Saturday or a Sunday (TRUE or FALSE). Use the weekday's name, not its number.
accepted: CASE DATENAME('weekday', [Start]) WHEN 'Saturday' THEN TRUE WHEN 'Sunday' THEN TRUE ELSE FALSE END
hints: DATENAME('weekday', date) returns the day's name, such as "Monday".
A session is on the weekend if its day is Saturday OR Sunday.
debrief: Weekday numbers depend on the start of the week, which comes from the data source unless you pass one; the names don't. OR is true when either side is, AND only when both are.
